source.title: When Does Legacy Data Start to Help? Emergent Transfer in Cross-Configuration Robot Learning
source.authors: Tao Wang; Hudson Hou; Ying-Dong Hu; Yufeng Liu; Qing-Hai Li; Yingjie Jiang; Ying-Zhi Wang; Cheng Ma; R. Wang; Yang Gao

record.file_problem: The paper is substantially present, though some extracted appendix figure text is garbled. The main experimental results and tables are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses a grokking-like analogy, but its results concern when legacy robot demonstrations improve co-training—not delayed generalization after overfitting or any of the specified grokking mechanisms.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own robot co-training results, recorded below as findings that fit none of the claim versions. They measure task success with and without legacy data at different standalone baselines; they do not measure training accuracy saturating before test accuracy rises. The authors describe training-loss curves as an indirect diagnostic, not a direct measurement of the proposed gradient-alignment mechanism.
record.test_reason: The paper calls its robot co-training pattern 'grokking-like' by analogy only. It measures how the gain from co-training with legacy data varies with standalone success rate across data settings. It does not track test accuracy over training time after training accuracy saturates. It runs no algorithmic datasets, circuit analysis, weight-norm or initialization manipulation, LLM training, or optimizer-artifact controls. The authors state the transition occurs across standalone performance, 'rather than as model scale or training time increases.'
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors find legacy data gives no measurable gain below a task-dependent transfer threshold, large gains just above it, and diminishing gains near saturation. They explain this with gradient alignment and residual uncertainty, propose a phase-aware data collection rule, and say the pattern only resembles grokking because it occurs across standalone performance rather than training time or scale.
record.recipe_differences: No original grokking method is reproduced; the study compares robot policies trained on new-hardware demonstrations alone with policies co-trained on legacy and new-hardware demonstrations.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured co-training gain varies with task, evaluated hardware configuration, Gen-2 data quality or budget, and standalone success rate.

fits_no_version.finding: Co-training gain from legacy robot data follows an inverted-U against standalone success rate on the new hardware. The gain is about 0 at low baselines (10%→10%), large at intermediate baselines (23.3%→86.7%; 51.7%→91.7%) and small near saturation (85%→93.3%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In cross-configuration robot co-training, legacy data helps only after the target configuration passes a task-dependent competence threshold, with diminishing gains near saturation.

record.problems: The study covers two hardware generations on one wheeled-humanoid platform, one VLA backbone, and a limited task set. The authors say direct per-source gradient alignment was not recorded; training-loss curves are only an indirect diagnostic. The proposed task-complexity/threshold relation is described as insufficiently validated to establish a scaling law.
record.rows_left_out: The paper's Figure 3 summarizes the phase pattern already represented by the individual table results. Table 7's early and refined pen-insertion entries duplicate results recorded in Tables 2 and 3, so they are not repeated. Figure 5's training-loss trajectories are indirect diagnostics, not measurements of delayed generalization or the claim versions.

untested.parts: No algorithmic dataset; no train/test accuracy curves over training time.
No circuit formation or progress measures. Training-loss curves (Fig. 5) are an indirect diagnostic of gradient alignment, not of delayed generalization.
Robot data, but no delayed generalization over training is measured, and no initialization scale, weight norm or lazy/rich manipulation.
VLA fine-tuning (Gemma-2B trunk), but there is no time-resolved delayed generalization after overfitting; only end-of-training success rates (40k steps) are reported.
No weight decay manipulation, critical dataset size, or ungrokking.
No comparison of learned algorithms across runs.
No optimizer or numerical artifact tests.

record.verdict_notes: Row states such as 'partial' and 'observed' describe the study's own co-training-gain construct, not any grokking version. All rows correctly carry versions ['none']. The grokking link is purely terminological, through a citation of Power et al. 2022.

versions.untested_parts: No small algorithmic dataset, training-accuracy saturation, or delayed test-accuracy rise is tested.
No gradual formation or removal of a generalizing circuit, Fourier algorithm, or continuous progress measure is tested.

The paper studies robot manipulation, but measures a change in co-training benefit with standalone competence, not grokking-like delayed generalization. It does not test initialization scale, weight norm, or a lazy-to-rich transition.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is studied.
No weight-decay or low-norm efficiency account, critical dataset size, or ungrokking is tested.
The paper does not identify or compare learned algorithms across runs.
The paper does not test adaptive-optimizer instability or floating-point/softmax artifacts as explanations of grokking.
